claim: Caenorhabditis elegans uses feedback from the motor circuit to a sensory processing interneuron to sustain its motor state during thermotactic navigation.
source: Here, we report that Caenorhabditis elegans uses feedback from the motor circuit to a sensory processing interneuron to sustain its motor state during thermotactic navigation.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including calcium imaging and behavioral assays.

claim: The AIY interneuron encodes both temperature and motor state information.
source: By imaging circuit activity in behaving animals, we show that a principal postsynaptic partner of the AFD thermosensory neuron, the AIY interneuron, encodes both temperature and motor state information.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2E-G and Figure 3A-B.

claim: The motor state representation in AIY is a corollary discharge signal.
source: By optogenetic and genetic manipulation of this circuit, we demonstrate that the motor state representation in AIY is a corollary discharge signal.
evidence: Demonstrated through optogenetic experiments (Figure 4C-F) and genetic manipulations (Figure 4A-B).

claim: RIM is required for the corollary discharge signal to AIY.
source: RIM, an interneuron that is connected with premotor interneurons, is required for this corollary discharge.
evidence: Shown by ablation experiments where RIM removal eliminates motor representation in AIY (Figure 4A-B, Figure 5A-C).

claim: Ablation of RIM eliminates the motor representation in AIY.
source: Ablation of RIM eliminates the motor representation in AIY, allows thermosensory representations to reach downstream premotor interneurons, and reduces the animal's ability to sustain forward movements during thermotaxis.
evidence: Demonstrated by calcium imaging in RIM-ablated animals (Figure 5A-C).

claim: Ablation of RIM allows thermosensory representations to reach downstream premotor interneurons.
source: Ablation of RIM eliminates the motor representation in AIY, allows thermosensory representations to reach downstream premotor interneurons, and reduces the animal's ability to sustain forward movements during thermotaxis.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A where AVA and motor neurons show thermosensory responses in RIM-ablated animals.

claim: Ablation of RIM reduces the animal's ability to sustain forward movements during thermotaxis.
source: Ablation of RIM eliminates the motor representation in AIY, allows thermosensory representations to reach downstream premotor interneurons, and reduces the animal's ability to sustain forward movements during thermotaxis.
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral assays showing reduced run duration in RIM-ablated animals (Figure 6C).

claim: Feedback from the motor circuit to the sensory processing circuit underlies a positive feedback mechanism to generate persistent neural activity.
source: We propose that feedback from the motor circuit to the sensory processing circuit underlies a positive feedback mechanism to generate persistent neural activity and sustained behavioral patterns in a sensorimotor transformation.
evidence: Supported by modeling results (Figure 7) and experimental observations of persistent AIY activity (Figure 3).

claim: C. elegans cultivated at 25°C exhibit biased random walk towards warmer temperatures on a 19-23°C gradient.
source: Consistent with earlier reports, these animals exhibited biased random walk and klinotaxis towards warmer temperatures (Figure 1B; Luo et al., 2014a; Yamaguchi et al., 2018)
evidence: Shown in Figure 1A-B with behavioral trajectories and quantification.

claim: During positive thermotaxis, runs that pointed in favorable directions were lengthened.
source: Consistent with earlier reports, these animals exhibited biased random walk and klinotaxis towards warmer temperatures (Figure 1B; Luo et al., 2014a; Yamaguchi et al., 2018): runs that pointed in favorable directions were lengthened (Figure 1B)
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1B showing run duration as a function of direction.

claim: During positive thermotaxis, forward heading angles gradually reoriented towards temperatures that correspond to prior experience.
source: forward heading angles gradually reoriented towards temperatures that correspond to prior experience (Figure 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1B right panel with velocity as a function of heading angle.

claim: Without a temperature gradient, there was no evident modulation of either run length or heading angle.
source: Without a temperature gradient, there was no evident modulation of either run length or heading angle (Figure 1B).
evidence: Control data shown in Figure 1B bottom panels.

claim: Most runs during thermotaxis involve periods of both warming and cooling stimuli because of frequent changes in movement direction.
source: Most runs – even those that orient the animal towards warmer temperatures – will involve periods of both warming and cooling stimuli because of frequent changes in movement direction (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1D showing distribution of dT/dt during forward runs.

claim: C. elegans reveals an ability to sustain forward movement up temperature gradients despite transient cooling fluctuations.
source: Thus, C. elegans reveals an ability to sustain forward movement up temperature gradients despite transient cooling fluctuations.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral data showing sustained runs despite cooling periods (Figure 1C-D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: AFD is the thermosensory neuron that mediates both positive and negative thermotaxis.
source: AFD is the thermosensory neuron that mediates both positive and negative thermotaxis (Luo et al., 2014a; Hawk et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on cited previous studies.

claim: AIY is a first-layer interneuron specifically required for positive thermotaxis.
source: Its principal chemical synaptic partner, AIY, is a first-layer interneuron specifically required for positive thermotaxis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies and circuit anatomy.

claim: AIY responds to temperature variations due to excitatory input from AFD.
source: AIY responds to temperature variations due to excitatory input from AFD (Clark et al., 2006; Clark et al., 2007; Narayan et al., 2011; Hawk et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on cited previous studies.

claim: AIY has been shown to promote the speed and duration of forward locomotion.
source: AIY has been shown to promote the speed and duration of forward locomotion (Li et al., 2014; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003).
evidence: Based on cited previous studies.

claim: AFD's activity phase locks to periodic variations in temperatures, rising upon warming and falling upon cooling.
source: As previously reported (Clark et al., 2006), AFD's activity phase locks to periodic variations in temperatures, rising upon warming and falling upon cooling (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C-D with calcium imaging data.

claim: AFD activity did not covary with transitions between forward run and reversal states.
source: AFD activity did not covary with transitions between forward run and reversal states (Figure 2C), indicating that motor commands arise downstream of the thermosensory neuron.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2C-D where AFD activity only correlates with temperature, not motor state.

claim: Motor commands arise downstream of the thermosensory neuron AFD.
source: AFD activity did not covary with transitions between forward run and reversal states (Figure 2C), indicating that motor commands arise downstream of the thermosensory neuron.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AFD does not encode motor state.

claim: During forward movements, AIY's calcium activity on average increased upon warming and decreased upon cooling with substantial trial-to-trial variability.
source: During forward movements, AIY's calcium activity on average increased upon warming and decreased upon cooling with substantial trial-to-trial variability (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E-G with calcium imaging data.

claim: During reversals, AIY's thermosensory responses were largely absent.
source: During reversals, these responses were largely absent (Figure 2E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E-G where AIY shows minimal activity during reversals.

claim: Motor circuit neurons examined exhibited little to no phase-locked response to thermosensory stimulation.
source: Unlike AFD and AIY, all motor circuit neurons that we examined exhibited little to no phase-locked response to thermosensory stimulation.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E-F where motor neurons show no correlation with temperature oscillations.

claim: Motor neurons reliably encoded the forward versus reversal movement states.
source: Instead, motor neurons reliably encoded the forward versus reversal movement states (Figure 2E, F, see the stimulus cross-correlation plots).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E-F with activity patterns and cross-correlations.

claim: AVA calcium activity exhibited high and low states that correlated with backward and forward movement, respectively.
source: In animals subjected to oscillating thermosensory stimulation, AVA calcium activity exhibited high and low states that correlated with backward and forward movement, respectively (Figure 2E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E with AVA activity traces.

claim: AVA activity pattern is consistent with its known activity profile in the absence of thermal stimulation and its functional role in promoting the reversal state.
source: This observation is consistent with the known activity profile of AVA in the absence of thermal stimulation and its functional role in promoting the reversal state (Chalfie et al., 1985; Kawano et al., 2011; McCormick et al., 2011; Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited previous studies.

claim: RIM interneuron was selectively active during reversals.
source: Similarly, the RIM interneuron was selectively active during reversals and its activity positively correlated with AVA activity.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E with RIM activity traces.

claim: RIM activity positively correlated with AVA activity.
source: Similarly, the RIM interneuron was selectively active during reversals and its activity positively correlated with AVA activity.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2I with cross-correlation data.

claim: The head motor neurons RME, SMDD, and SMDV were selectively active during forward runs.
source: The head motor neurons RME, SMDD, and SMDV were selectively active during forward runs.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E with motor neuron activity traces.

claim: The SMD neurons exhibited alternating activity patterns.
source: The SMD neurons exhibited alternating activity patterns, consistent with previous reports (Hendricks et al., 2012).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2E and supported by cited previous study.

claim: For positive thermotaxis, the sensorimotor transformation progresses through three layers of processing.
source: Together, these observations indicate that, for positive thermotaxis, the sensorimotor transformation progresses through three layers of processing (Figure 2A): the thermosensory neuron encodes only thermal stimuli; the first layer interneuron encodes both thermal stimuli and motor states; the premotor and motor neurons primarily encode the motor state.
evidence: Inferred from the combined calcium imaging data in Figure 2.

claim: The activity of all six neurons continued to be modulated by locomotory state under constant temperature in the same way as when exposed to oscillating temperature.
source: We found that the activity of all six neurons continued to be modulated by locomotory state in the same way as when exposed to oscillating temperature.
evidence: Shown in Figure 2H comparing activity under constant vs oscillating temperature.

claim: The pairwise cross-correlation between neurons remained the same under both oscillatory and constant temperature.
source: Furthermore, the pairwise cross-correlation between neurons remained the same under both oscillatory and constant temperature (Figure 2I).
evidence: Shown in Figure 2I with cross-correlation data.

claim: The widespread encoding of motor state in neurons downstream of AFD does not require thermosensory input.
source: These observations indicate that the widespread encoding of motor state in neurons downstream of AFD does not require thermosensory input and may instead reflect an intrinsic circuit property.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that motor state encoding persists under constant temperature (Figure 2H-I).

claim: AIY activity consistently rises at the beginning of forward runs and decays at the onset of reversals in animals exposed to either constant or oscillating temperatures.
source: In animals exposed to either constant or oscillating temperatures, AIY activity consistently rises at the beginning of forward runs and decays at the onset of reversals (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3A-B with event-triggered averages.

claim: AIY exhibited persistent activation, the duration of which coincided reliably with that of the forward run state.
source: Moreover, AIY exhibited persistent activation, the duration of which coincided reliably with that of the forward run state (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with correlation analysis.

claim: AIY activity remained strongly coupled to the motor state despite blocking vesicle release from AIY through cell-specific expression of tetanus toxin.
source: Despite the lack of synaptic and dense-core-vesicle-dependent chemical release (Whim et al., 1997), AIY activity remained strongly coupled to the motor state, implying that AIY must receive the motor state signal.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3C with AIY::TeTx experiments.

claim: AIY must receive the motor state signal.
source: Despite the lack of synaptic and dense-core-vesicle-dependent chemical release (Whim et al., 1997), AIY activity remained strongly coupled to the motor state, implying that AIY must receive the motor state signal.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking AIY output does not eliminate motor state encoding in AIY.

claim: C. elegans movement is not required for AIY activity to reflect motor state.
source: C. elegans movement is not required for AIY activity to reflect motor state, arguing against proprioception.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3D with immobilized animal experiments.

claim: Proprioception does not underlie the calcium response in AIY.
source: C. elegans movement is not required for AIY activity to reflect motor state, arguing against proprioception.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing motor state encoding persists in immobilized animals (Figure 3D).

claim: Ablating AIB did not abolish the motor state representation in AIY.
source: We found that ablating AIB did not abolish the motor state representation in AIY (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A-B with ablation experiments.

claim: Removal of the premotor interneurons AVA or AVB alone did not abolish motor state representation in AIY.
source: Neither did the removal of the premotor interneurons AVA or AVB alone (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B with ablation experiments.

claim: AIY lost its motor state representation when RIM was ablated either by itself or in combination with other premotor interneurons.
source: However, AIY lost its motor state representation when we ablated RIM either by itself or in combination with other premotor interneurons (Figure 4A, B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C with ablation experiments.

claim: RIM activity has been shown to be correlated with the AVA premotor interneuron that promotes reversals and anti-correlated with the AVB premotor interneuron that promotes forward runs.
source: RIM activity has been shown to be correlated with the AVA premotor interneuron that promotes reversals and anti-correlated with the AVB premotor interneuron that promotes forward runs (Kawano et al., 2011; Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited previous studies.

claim: RIM has been shown to promote long reversals.
source: RIM has been shown to promote long reversals (Gray et al., 2005) and to suppress head oscillations during reversals (Alkema et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on cited previous studies.

claim: RIM promotes the stability of forward runs when hyperpolarized.
source: A recent study demonstrated that RIM also promotes the stability of forward runs when hyperpolarized (Sordillo et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on cited recent study.

claim: Activation of AVB using the light-gated opsin chrimson triggered an increase in AIY calcium levels.
source: Activation of AVB using the light-gated opsin chrimson triggered an increase in AIY calcium levels (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C-D with optogenetic experiments.

claim: Activation of AVA triggered a decrease in AIY calcium levels.
source: Activation of AVA (Klapoetke et al., 2014) triggered a decrease in AIY calcium levels (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4E-F with optogenetic experiments.

claim: When RIM was ablated, AIY calcium signals no longer responded to optogenetic activation of either AVA or AVB.
source: When RIM was ablated, AIY calcium signals no longer responded to optogenetic activation of either AVA or AVB, suggesting that RIM is part of the CD pathway from the motor circuit to AIY.
evidence: Shown in Figure 4C-F with optogenetic experiments in RIM-ablated animals.

claim: RIM is part of the CD pathway from the motor circuit to AIY.
source: When RIM was ablated, AIY calcium signals no longer responded to optogenetic activation of either AVA or AVB, suggesting that RIM is part of the CD pathway from the motor circuit to AIY.
evidence: Inferred from optogenetic experiments showing RIM is necessary for motor-related signals to reach AIY.

claim: Without RIM, AIY activity no longer reflected or depended on the motor state.
source: Without RIM, AIY activity no longer reflected or depended on the motor state, but the premotor interneurons AVA continued to encode the backward and forward movement, albeit with reduced bimodal activity (Figure 5A, C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A, C with calcium imaging in RIM-ablated animals.

claim: Without RIM, the premotor interneurons AVA continued to encode the backward and forward movement, albeit with reduced bimodal activity.
source: Without RIM, AIY activity no longer reflected or depended on the motor state, but the premotor interneurons AVA continued to encode the backward and forward movement, albeit with reduced bimodal activity (Figure 5A, C).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A, C with AVA activity in RIM-ablated animals.

claim: RIM is not essential for generating motor commands.
source: Thus, RIM is not essential for generating motor commands, but is necessary to relay motor information to AIY, a first-layer interneuron.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that motor states persist in RIM-ablated animals.

claim: RIM is necessary to relay motor information to AIY.
source: Thus, RIM is not essential for generating motor commands, but is necessary to relay motor information to AIY, a first-layer interneuron.
evidence: Demonstrated by ablation and optogenetic experiments (Figure 4, Figure 5).

claim: RIM expresses VGLUT3/EAT-4, indicating the potential involvement of glutamatergic synaptic transmission.
source: RIM expresses VGLUT3/EAT-4, indicating the potential involvement of glutamatergic synaptic transmission (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on cited previous study.

claim: RIM synthesizes tyramine, a monoamine neuromodulator.
source: RIM also synthesizes tyramine, a monoamine neuromodulator (Alkema et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on cited previous study.

claim: AIY activity co-varied with the motor state in all mutants tested for synaptic transmission.
source: AIY activity co-varied with the motor state in all mutants, but the difference in AIY activity between the forward run and reversal states was less distinct in mutants defective for vesicular monoamine transport (VMAT/cat-1) or tyramine synthesis (TDC/tdc-1) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B with mutant analysis.

claim: The difference in AIY activity between the forward run and reversal states was less distinct in mutants defective for vesicular monoamine transport (VMAT/cat-1) or tyramine synthesis (TDC/tdc-1).
source: AIY activity co-varied with the motor state in all mutants, but the difference in AIY activity between the forward run and reversal states was less distinct in mutants defective for vesicular monoamine transport (VMAT/cat-1) or tyramine synthesis (TDC/tdc-1) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B with mutant analysis.

claim: Blocking vesicle fusion in RIM by expressing TeTx attenuated the motor state representation in AIY.
source: Blocking vesicle fusion in RIM by expressing TeTx (Ptdc-1::TeTx) also attenuated the motor state representation in AIY (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B with TeTx experiments.

claim: Neuronal communication that is independent of classic chemical synaptic transmission is likely involved in relaying CD to AIY.
source: Since perturbation of chemical synaptic transmission did not fully abolish motor-related activity in AIY, neuronal communication that is independent of classic chemical synaptic transmission is likely involved in relaying CD to AIY.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking chemical transmission does not fully eliminate motor state encoding in AIY.

claim: The joint representation of sensory and motor signals in AIY arises from separate sources: feedforward input from AFD and feedback from the motor circuit that is dependent on RIM.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the joint representation of sensory and motor signals in AIY arises from separate sources: feedforward input from AFD and feedback from the motor circuit that is dependent on RIM.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of AFD imaging, RIM ablation, and optogenetic experiments.

claim: When RIM-ablated animals were subjected to oscillating temperatures, AIY activity was no longer coupled to the motor state, but instead reliably tracked temperature fluctuations during both forward and backward movements.
source: When RIM-ablated animals were subjected to oscillating temperatures, AIY activity was no longer coupled to the motor state, but instead reliably tracked temperature fluctuations during both forward and backward movements (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A-B with calcium imaging in RIM-ablated animals.

claim: Under oscillating temperature, the average duration of AIY activation was shortened in RIM-ablated animals compared to wild type.
source: Under oscillating temperature, the average duration of AIY activation was shortened compared to wild type, though no significant difference was observed under constant temperature (Figure 5D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B with duration analysis.

claim: When RIM was ablated, the representation of thermosensory oscillations was detected in the activity pattern of the AVA premotor interneuron and the head motor neurons RME and SMDV.
source: When RIM was ablated, we were also able to detect the representation of thermosensory oscillations in the activity pattern of the AVA premotor interneuron and the head motor neurons RME and SMDV (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5A with cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The loss of the RIM-dependent motor signal resulted in a sensorimotor circuit that becomes more susceptible to fluctuations in thermosensory input.
source: This observation suggests that the loss of the RIM-dependent motor signal resulted in a sensorimotor circuit that becomes more susceptible to fluctuations in thermosensory input.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that thermosensory signals reach motor neurons in RIM-ablated animals.

claim: Without RIM and the motor state encoding in AIY, fluctuations in thermosensory inputs are readily propagated to the motor circuit.
source: Without RIM and the motor state encoding in AIY, fluctuations in thermosensory inputs are readily propagated to the motor circuit.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that motor neurons show thermosensory responses in RIM-ablated animals (Figure 5A).

claim: The RIM-dependent CD may play an important role in sustaining neural activity states through fluctuating sensory inputs.
source: Thus, the RIM-dependent CD may play an important role in sustaining neural activity states through fluctuating sensory inputs.
evidence: Inferred from the combined neural and behavioral data showing reduced persistence in RIM-ablated animals.

claim: RIM-ablated animals exhibited an overall reduction in thermotaxis bias compared to wild-type animals.
source: Compared to wild-type animals, RIM-ablated animals exhibited an overall reduction in thermotaxis bias (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6B with behavioral assay data.

claim: RIM-ablated animals were specifically defective in their ability to sustain forward locomotion when moving up the thermal gradient.
source: These animals were specifically defective in their ability to sustain forward locomotion when moving up the thermal gradient, while their ability to gradually modify heading angle during a forward run remained intact (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6C with run duration analysis.

claim: RIM-ablated animals' ability to gradually modify heading angle during a forward run remained intact.
source: These animals were specifically defective in their ability to sustain forward locomotion when moving up the thermal gradient, while their ability to gradually modify heading angle during a forward run remained intact (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A with angular velocity analysis.

claim: At constant temperature, run durations are similar between wild-type and RIM-ablated animals.
source: At constant temperature, run durations are similar between wild-type and RIM-ablated animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B with behavioral data.

claim: The loss of RIM specifically disrupted the animal's ability to sustain forward runs up temperature gradients.
source: Thus, the loss of RIM specifically disrupted the animal's ability to sustain forward runs up temperature gradients.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of RIM-ablated animals on gradients vs constant temperature.

claim: Cooling induced reversals at a higher probability in RIM-ablated animals compared to the wild type.
source: Overall, cooling induced reversals at a higher probability in RIM-ablated animals compared to the wild type.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6D-F with analysis of cooling effects on behavior.

claim: The difference in cooling-induced reversals was particularly notable for persistent periods of cooling lasting from 7 to 30 s.
source: This difference was particularly notable for persistent periods of cooling lasting from 7 to 30 s (Figure 6E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6F with quantification of cooling effects.

claim: Forward runs in RIM-ablated animals are more likely to end after a period of cooling regardless of run length compared to the wild type.
source: We found that, compared to the wild type, forward runs in RIM-ablated animals are more likely to end after a period of cooling regardless of run length (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E with behavioral analysis.

claim: The positive feedback model exhibited stable high and low states in both the interneuron and the motor neuron when exposed to oscillating inputs.
source: When exposed to oscillating inputs, the positive feedback model exhibited stable high and low states in both the interneuron and the motor neuron.
evidence: Shown in Figure 7B with model simulations.

claim: The autocorrelative timescale of states in the positive feedback model outlasted the oscillatory period of the input signal.
source: The autocorrelative timescale of these states (a measure of persistence) outlasted the oscillatory period of the input signal (Figure 7B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7B with autocorrelation analysis.

claim: In models with no feedback or negative feedback, the oscillatory signal remained evident in both the interneuron and the motor neuron.
source: This was not the case for the models with no feedback or negative feedback where the oscillatory signal remained evident in both the interneuron and the motor neuron (Figure 7B).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7B with model simulations.

claim: The positive feedback model more effectively drove migration up the thermal gradient than the model with no feedback.
source: The positive feedback model more effectively drove migration up the thermal gradient than the model with no feedback.
evidence: Shown in Figure 7C-D with simulated trajectories and thermotaxis bias.

claim: The negative feedback model exhibited less effective thermotaxis than the no feedback model.
source: In contrast, the negative feedback model exhibited less effective thermotaxis than the no feedback model (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7C-D with simulated trajectories and thermotaxis bias.

claim: The duration of forward runs was overall significantly longer and exhibited stronger dependence of run duration on run direction in the positive feedback model compared to the alternative models.
source: The duration of forward runs was overall significantly longer and exhibited stronger dependence of run duration on run direction in the positive feedback model compared to the alternative models (Figure 7E).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7E with simulation results.

claim: Forward runs were much more likely to terminate after a period of cooling in the no feedback model compared to the positive feedback model.
source: Lastly, forward runs were much more likely to terminate after a period of cooling in the no feedback model compared to the positive feedback model, consistent with experimental observations in RIM-ablated animals.
evidence: Shown in Figure 7F-G with simulation results.

claim: The positive feedback model best explained the neural activity and behavioral data.
source: Thus, the positive feedback model best explained the neural activity and behavioral data.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of model predictions with experimental observations.

claim: CD in the form of positive feedback promotes persistent circuit activity states and effective navigation during time-varying thermosensory inputs.
source: These results indicate that CD in the form of positive feedback promotes persistent circuit activity states and effective navigation during time-varying thermosensory inputs.
evidence: Inferred from the combined modeling and experimental results.

claim: CD prevents periods of forward locomotion from being curtailed by transient negative temperature fluctuations during positive thermotaxis up gradients.
source: During positive thermotaxis up gradients, C. elegans generates sustained periods of forward locomotion that carry it up temperature gradients; CD prevents these periods of forward locomotion from being curtailed by transient negative temperature fluctuations.
evidence: Inferred from the combined behavioral and neural data showing reduced persistence in RIM-ablated animals.

claim: Recurrent circuitry has a prevalent role in persistent neural activities and behavioral states in mice and flies.
source: In mice and flies, recurrent circuitry has a prevalent role in persistent neural activities and behavioral states.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: In many systems, CD has a role in suppressing neural or behavioral responses.
source: In many systems, CD has a role in suppressing neural or behavioral responses.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from the literature on corollary discharge.

claim: CD is able to reinforce the behavioral response to a sensory input.
source: In contrast, we show that CD is also able to reinforce the behavioral response to a sensory input.
evidence: Demonstrated by the experimental results showing positive feedback from motor to sensory circuits.

claim: AIY is postsynaptic to many sensory neurons and is required for navigation in other modalities.
source: Because AIY is postsynaptic to many sensory neurons and is required for navigation in other modalities (Wakabayashi et al., 2004; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Luo et al., 2014a), CD-based feedback to AIY might play a general role in many different sensorimotor pathways.
evidence: Based on cited previous studies.

claim: CD-based feedback to AIY might play a general role in many different sensorimotor pathways.
source: Because AIY is postsynaptic to many sensory neurons and is required for navigation in other modalities (Wakabayashi et al., 2004; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Luo et al., 2014a), CD-based feedback to AIY might play a general role in many different sensorimotor pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the general role of AIY in multiple sensory modalities.

claim: In a recent study of olfactory responses in immobilized animals, RIM was shown to send feedback input to AIB.
source: In a recent study of olfactory responses in immobilized animals, RIM was also shown to send feedback input to AIB, another sensory processing interneuron whose activity promotes the reversal state (Gordus et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited previous study.

claim: In the olfactory pathway, RIM activity was required to correlate the activity of AIB and the AVA premotor interneuron.
source: In the olfactory pathway, RIM activity was required to correlate the activity of AIB and the AVA premotor interneuron.
evidence: Based on cited previous study (Gordus et al., 2015).

claim: Silencing RIM led to more reliable odor-evoked response in AIB and odor-induced initiation of forward runs.
source: Silencing RIM led to more reliable odor-evoked response in AIB and odor-induced initiation of forward runs.
evidence: Based on cited previous study (Gordus et al., 2015).

claim: The effect of silencing RIM in the olfactory sensorimotor pathway mirrors the impact of RIM ablation on AIY during positive thermotaxis.
source: Thus, the effect of silencing RIM in the olfactory sensorimotor pathway mirrors the impact of RIM ablation on AIY, during positive thermotaxis, shown in this study.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with previous study (Gordus et al., 2015).

claim: CD plays a wide role in promoting persistent states in sensorimotor transformation.
source: Together, this evidence suggests a wide role for CD in promoting persistent states in sensorimotor transformation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined evidence from thermotaxis and olfaction studies.

claim: Motor behavior can significantly impact sensory processing across species.
source: Our findings add to a growing body of literature from across species that motor behavior can significantly impact sensory processing (Petreanu et al., 2009; Zagha et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2014; Schneider et al., 2014; Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015; Ouellette et al., 2018; Musall et al., 2019; Stringer et al., 2019; Salkoff et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on cited previous studies across multiple species.

claim: An explicit dependence of sensory encoding on behavioral states has been shown to contribute to variability in stimulus-evoked neural and behavioral responses.
source: An explicit dependence of sensory encoding on behavioral states has been shown to contribute to variability in stimulus-evoked neural and behavioral responses (Fontanini and Katz, 2008; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited previous studies.

claim: In mice performing visual and auditory tasks, cortex-wide neural activity can be dominated by movement-related signals, many of which are uninstructed.
